paras: The Simmons gang threat against Boley was a reported threat in August 1905 by the outlaw Andy Simmons to attack Boley, Oklahoma, a Black town, and kill its Black officials and residents in revenge for his brother's death and his brothers' arrests. Extra police and marshals guarded the town, and many Black residents of Boley and nearby Paden were said to be leaving their homes. No attack was reported, and the threat appeared only in the Guthrie Daily Leader.

Some days earlier, a deputy marshal went out from Boley to arrest Dick Simmons, who was wanted for horse stealing. The Boley Progress named the officer as W. R. Shaver, "better known as Dick Shaver," a U.S. deputy marshal who had also been appointed Boley's city marshal, while the Guthrie wire called him Ed Shaffer. According to the wire, Simmons stepped from behind a clump of bushes and shot the marshal, who killed Simmons before dying himself five minutes later. The Boley Progress said each man fired two shots, that Shaver lived about half an hour, and that a coroner's jury returned a verdict on those facts.

Two younger Simmons brothers were then arrested, one of them, Lewis, with the help of officials at Paden. At Dick Simmons's funeral, the Guthrie Daily Leader reported, his mother said that "Andy will have revenge."

On 21 August the Guthrie Daily Leader stated that it was "authoritatively reported" that Andy Simmons, who had a price on his head for the murder of a deputy marshal, had returned to his home near Boley. He was said to have sent word to the town's "colored officials and inhabitants" that they should prepare to die, and to be organizing "a posse of bad men" to "kill off the negroes." On Saturday night an extra force of police and marshals was posted on the outskirts of Boley to prevent a surprise attack. At Paden, the officials who had helped arrest Lewis Simmons armed themselves, and many Black residents of both towns and of farms near the Simmons ranch left for other towns.
No report of an attack on either town, or of the capture of Andy Simmons, appears in the coverage.

Only the Guthrie Daily Leader reported the threat, under the headline "Two Towns in Terror" and the deck "Negro Populace Fear Attack From Criminal Gang Seeking Revenge." While presenting the threat as authoritative, the paper blamed the confusion and the officers' difficulty in organizing a defense largely on "Superstition and ignorance" and on "incredible rumors started by irresponsible persons."

The earlier shooting travelled more widely as a Guthrie wire brief headed "Kill Each Other," which ran in Texas papers at Waxahachie, Bryan and Palestine on 18 and 19 August and identified Boley as "a negro settlement." A rewritten version in The Berne Witness of Indiana on 25 August described Dick Simmons as "a negro."

In the Black press, the Boley Progress gave the fullest account of the shooting, describing Shaver as "both widely and favorably known throughout the Territory" and noting his burial under the auspices of a local lodge. The Oklahoma Safeguard carried a short, garbled Guthrie item on the two deaths on 24 August. Neither Black paper mentioned a threat against Boley.

The papers disagree on the marshal's name, which appears as Shaver in the Boley Progress and as Shaffer, Shafer or Schaffer in the Guthrie reports; the local paper, which knew him as a Boley resident, is the likelier source on this point. The timing also differs, since the Boley Progress of 17 August reported Shaver already buried on Tuesday, while the Guthrie Daily Leader placed the shooting on "last Wednesday."

reader.title: Simmons gang threat against Boley
bases: The only report of the episode describes a threat, sent by an outlaw seeking revenge, to attack Boley and kill its Black residents, with guards posted and residents leaving, but no attack or injury is reported [A5].

No one was reported killed in the threatened attack; the threat came from an outlaw said to be organizing 'a posse of bad men' to avenge his brother's death and his brothers' arrests, a stated motive of revenge rather than a claim of justice, and no attack is reported [A5]. The preceding deaths of the marshal and Dick Simmons were an exchange of gunfire during an arrest attempt, not a mob killing [A1, A3].

The threat, the guards and the flight of residents appear only in the Guthrie Daily Leader [A5]; the preceding shooting is corroborated by the Boley Progress and the Guthrie wire [A1, A3, A6], none of which mention a threat.

accounts.label: Guthrie Daily Leader
accounts.gist: Andy Simmons, angered by his brother's killing and his brothers' arrests, sent word that Boley's Black officials and residents should prepare to die and was organizing a gang to attack; guards were posted and residents fled.

accounts.label: Guthrie wire
accounts.gist: Deputy marshal Ed Shaffer, sent to arrest Dick Simmons for horse stealing, was shot from ambush near Boley, killed Simmons, and died five minutes later.

accounts.label: Boley Progress (local Black paper)
accounts.gist: Marshal W. R. Shaver, going to arrest Simmons for horse stealing, was fired on without warning; each man fired two shots and both died; a coroner's jury confirmed the facts.

framing.detail: The Guthrie Daily Leader's 'Two Towns in Terror / Negro Populace Fear Attack' reported the threat as authoritative but attributed the town's confusion to the 'Superstition and ignorance' of residents and 'incredible rumors'.
Texas and Indiana papers ran the Guthrie brief 'Kill Each Other' on the shooting, identifying Boley as 'a negro settlement', without any mention of a threat.
The Boley Progress eulogized Shaver as 'widely and favorably known' and reported the shooting and burial; neither it nor the Oklahoma Safeguard mentioned a threat to the town.

versions.value: W. R. Shaver, 'better known as Dick Shaver'

conflicts.note: The local Black paper, which knew him as a Boley resident, gives Shaver; the Guthrie papers give Shaffer variants.
The Boley Progress issue date and its Tuesday burial do not fit a Wednesday shooting; the issue may have appeared after its nominal date.

info: Threat reported on 21 August 1905; extra police and marshals guarded Boley's outskirts on the preceding Saturday night (19 August).
Boley, described as 'a negro settlement'; also Paden, a nearby town where residents were said to be terrified.
No victims; the threat was directed at 'the colored officials and inhabitants' of Boley.
Andy Simmons, described as 'the most desperate of the entire Simmons gang of outlaws', reportedly organizing 'a posse of bad men'.
No report of an attack on Boley or of the capture of Andy Simmons appears in the coverage.
